## Chapter One: The Quiet Before

The house had a soft, golden light on the windows, like something had gently warmed the walls.

I sat on the rug in the corner, my feet tucked beneath me. My feet were small and warm, and I didn’t notice them. The book was open on the coffee table, its pages yellow with the pages I had already read.

For a long time, I did not want to read it. I wanted to listen to the sound of the house settling into itself.

Outside, the street was alive with small noises. A pigeon landed on a nearby branch and made a tiny flap of wings. A car passed by with a long, steady hum, like a big animal moving through the neighborhood. A woman walked past with a red scarf, and the scarf seemed to carry a little wind.

I watched the pigeon again. It landed and tapped its head against the branch, then looked up at the sky.

The sky was blue and full of clouds. Some clouds looked like little cotton balls, and some looked like pieces of paper. One cloud was shaped like a cat, and it was smiling.

I smiled back.

I was sitting in the corner of the living room, and the house was already full of quiet. It had a soft light. It had small, happy noises. It had a cat-shaped cloud.

The book was still open. I did not want to read it. I wanted to listen to the house.

I closed my eyes and listened.

The house breathed.

It took in the cool air. It let out a little sigh.

Then it settled down.

And I, sitting in the corner, did not know what to do with my hands.

The dish featured a piece of skin-on chicken cooked in a gentle skin-on pan with apple and carrot chunks, rosemary, and a splash of chicken stock until the chicken was golden and tender. A little lemon juice and salt helped the flavors come together.

She arranged the chicken and vegetables in a shallow bowl and served it with crusty bread and a glass of orange juice. The kitchen filled with the warm aroma of roasted apple and rosemary, giving her morning a cozy, welcoming feel.

The occasion was a quiet moment of self-care after a busy day of organizing groceries and preparing meals. It was neither a formal celebration nor a special family gathering, but an ordinary Tuesday treated with care. Ingrid had made it special by preparing it herself—simple, practical, and full of warmth.
